lesson_title: Sweat Is Not Work: The Work-Energy Theorem
hook_text: Hold 50 kg of cement on your shoulders for ten minutes. Physics says you did ZERO work.
clip_script: Hold a fifty-kilogram bag of cement on your shoulders, dead still, for ten minutes. Legs shaking, back burning. And physics looks at you and says: zero work done. Zero! Because in physics, work isn't effort — it's force times distance ALONG the force. Your push is up, the bag went nowhere: no distance, no work. Walk it across the yard at the same height? Still zero — your force is up, the motion is sideways, and a sideways force contributes nothing. Only when you lift the bag onto the bakkie does the meter start running: force up, motion up, work done, energy delivered. And lowering it gently? Your work is negative — you're draining energy out, which is why it lands softly. Now the payoff, the work-energy theorem: net work equals the change in kinetic energy. It's why doubling your speed quadruples your braking distance — energy grows with the SQUARE of speed, and friction must claw back four times the joules over four times the metres. Same brakes, four times the distance. That's not a road-safety poster. That's an equation.
visual_style: A strained figure holding a cement bag with a big counter stuck at zero joules; the counter finally spinning as the bag rises onto a bakkie; cut to two cars braking, one at 60 and one at 120, with energy bars and skid distances growing as squares.
mood: Wry and surprising, tightening into road-safety seriousness.
pacing: Comedy beat on the frozen zero counter, quick lift reveal, hard-hitting braking-distance finish.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and let energy do your physics homework for you.
